hero.headline: NASA announces Artemis III astronaut crew for Moon landing mission
hero.body:
NASA has announced significant changes to its Artemis program, shifting to a more cautious, step-by-step strategy for returning humans to the Moon. The new plan delays the crewed lunar landing to 2028 and introduces additional test missions before attempting to land astronauts on the lunar surface.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman unveiled the revised approach on Friday, citing technical challenges and safety concerns that prompted the agency to rethink its original timeline. "We've got to get back to basics," Isaacman told reporters. "We're going to get there in steps, continue to take down risk as we learn more and we roll that information into subsequent designs."

The changes come after an independent aerospace safety panel issued a sharp critique of NASA's original Artemis III plan, calling it too risky and recommending the agency reconsider its objectives. The panel expressed urgency given what it described as "demanding mission goals" that pushed the program too far too fast.

Under the revised schedule, Artemis II, which will send four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the Moon, has been postponed to April 1 at the earliest. The mission was previously scheduled for March 6. The delay follows recent technical problems, including a blockage discovered in the rocket's helium flow system and earlier hydrogen leaks from the Space Launch System rocket.

The new plan restructures the remaining missions significantly. Artemis III will no longer attempt a lunar landing. Instead, it will launch by mid-2027 as a low-Earth orbit test mission designed to validate essential technologies and give NASA flight experience with its advanced systems before committing astronauts to a landing attempt.

If testing proceeds successfully, a new Artemis IV mission would then conduct the actual moon landing in 2028. Isaacman compared this incremental approach to the original Apollo program, which completed two crewed lunar orbit missions before Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon in 1969.

NASA's long-term vision includes additional lunar landings with a target of Artemis V in 2028, followed by yearly moon missions thereafter. The program ultimately aims to establish a permanent lunar base near the Moon's south pole, with plans to deploy hopping drones and roving vehicles to support sustained exploration.

Isaacman emphasized that the revised approach represents the only viable path forward. "Everybody agrees this is the only way forward," he stated. "I know this is how NASA changed the world, and this is how NASA is going to do it again."

The strategic shift reflects NASA's commitment to prioritizing safety and technological readiness over accelerated timelines, acknowledging that sustainable lunar exploration requires thorough testing and validation at each stage.

cards.headline: US Missile Strikes Sanctioned Oil Tanker Off Oman
cards.teaser: A crew aboard an oil tanker issued a distress call after their vessel was hit by a missile fired from a US fighter jet.
cards.body:
A sanctioned oil tanker was struck by a missile fired from a US fighter jet in waters off Oman. The crew issued distress calls following the strike and were subsequently rescued from the damaged vessel.

US officials confirmed the strike on the ship, which was operating under international sanctions.

cards.headline: Israel Strikes Southern Lebanon After Brief Pause in Direct Iran Confrontation
cards.teaser: Israel launched new air strikes on southern Lebanon on Tuesday, targeting positions in the city of Tyre, one day after Israel and Iran pulled back from direct m.
cards.body:
Israel launched air strikes on southern Lebanon on Tuesday, targeting the city of Tyre, one day after stepping back from direct military confrontation with Iran. The attacks continued despite Iran's Monday warning that it could resume hostilities if strikes against its Lebanese ally Hezbollah do not stop.

The Israeli campaign against Hezbollah has complicated U.S.-Iran peace negotiations. Israel's willingness to continue operations against the Lebanese militia suggests that the pause in direct Israel-Iran hostilities does not extend to proxy forces. American officials are working to prevent the conflict from expanding, though Israel's continued strikes demonstrate the challenge of achieving a comprehensive ceasefire involving all regional parties.

cards.headline: House votes on $70 billion immigration enforcement funding bill
cards.teaser: Congress moves toward approving funding for ICE and border agencies through the end of Trump's presidency.
cards.body:
The House prepared to vote on a Republican immigration bill that would provide $70 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies. The measure would fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection through the remainder of the Trump presidency.

The vote represents the end of a months-long impasse in Congress over immigration funding. The bill represents a significant increase in resources for federal immigration enforcement operations.

cards.headline: Speaker Johnson meets with Trump as intelligence surveillance deadline looms
cards.teaser: Speaker Mike Johnson met with President Trump amid Democratic opposition to acting intelligence chief Bill Pulte that threatens foreign surveillance law reauthorization.
cards.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson met with President Trump on Tuesday morning as Democrats expressed serious concerns about Trump's appointment of Bill Pulte as acting Director of National Intelligence, threatening efforts to renew surveillance powers scheduled to expire at the end of the week.

The appointment has created a significant obstacle to reauthorizing Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which allows U.S. intelligence agencies to collect communications of foreign targets operating outside the country without a warrant. Congress faces a June 12 deadline to renew the authority.

Pulte, currently head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and a major Republican donor, has no intelligence background. His selection came days after Tulsi Gabbard departed from the DNI role. Senior Democrats immediately warned the appointment could collapse the fragile bipartisan agreement needed to extend Section 702.

Mark Warner, the Democratic vice-chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, criticized Pulte's qualifications. "What qualifications from my standpoint does Mr Pulte bring to the office? Well, he has shown that he is willing to do anything that President Trump wants, legal or otherwise," Warner said during a hearing Tuesday. In a subsequent interview, Warner stated that Pulte's appointment had upended what he described as an already difficult renewal process, saying "I do not have the confidence I had yesterday."

Democrats have made clear that support for a Section 702 extension could collapse unless Trump reconsiders the appointment. Warner reportedly asked Senate Majority Leader John Thune to use his influence with the White House to reverse the decision.

Thune offered a notably cool response to Trump's pick. He told reporters that the nation does not need a "weaponized" intelligence director and warned that Pulte would face "a lengthy road ahead" if nominated permanently.

Other senior Republicans have also pushed back. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate majority leader, said on Wednesday: "Anyone performing this role of such immense public trust must have the extensive national security experience required by statute, and no nominee who falls short of this requirement will earn my vote."

Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator from Connecticut, expressed concern that intelligence collection powers would now be controlled by someone with "a history of seeking out private information for political gain." Critics point to Pulte's tenure at the FHFA, where he leveled unproven fraud allegations against figures including Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook.

The current renewal bill, circulated by Senate Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton and Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, would extend Section 702 through June 2029 and include new penalties for intelligence abuses. The measure requires Democratic support to reach the 60-vote threshold needed for passage.

cards.headline: Uncrewed Vessel Rescues US Army Helicopter Crew Near Strait of Hormuz
cards.teaser: Two crew members of an Apache helicopter were recovered by a sea drone after their aircraft went down on Monday.
cards.body:
An unmanned vessel recovered two crew members from a US Army Apache helicopter that crashed near the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. US officials confirmed the autonomous watercraft successfully completed the rescue operation in the strategic waterway.

President Trump stated that both pilots were "fine" following the incident. The successful rescue highlights the operational capabilities of autonomous maritime systems in critical situations.

cards.headline: Stock Indexes Rise as Chip Rally Continues and Oil Prices Fall on Iran Deal Progress
cards.body:
Major US stock indexes climbed as chip stocks extended their rally and oil prices retreated following statements from President Trump about potential progress in negotiations with Iran. The market movements reflected investor optimism about both the technology sector and prospects for easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.

Stock markets across Asia and Europe rebounded after days of heavy losses driven by Middle East tensions. South Korea's KOSPI index rose by almost 10%, while Japan's Nikkei gained 1.9%. The broader MSCI Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan jumped 2.7%. This recovery followed a particularly difficult period, with South Korea's KOSPI posting its biggest ever fall of 12% earlier in the week.

Chip stocks led the gains in the technology sector, continuing a momentum that has benefited from sustained demand and positive sentiment around artificial intelligence applications. South Korean semiconductor manufacturers, which supply two-thirds of global memory chips, saw their stocks rebound along with broader market recovery. However, industry leaders have expressed concerns about the potential for prolonged conflict in Iran to disrupt supplies of important semiconductor manufacturing materials and drive up energy costs.

Oil prices pulled back from recent highs after Trump indicated the US and Iran were moving toward a potential deal, though he provided no specific details about timing or terms. The retreat in crude prices came after Israel and Iran agreed to halt strikes against each other, reducing immediate concerns about supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf region. Brent crude had previously risen to $84 a barrel following reports of attacks on US oil tankers in the region.

Energy markets had experienced significant volatility as the conflict escalated, with traders pricing in risks to oil infrastructure and shipping routes. The prospect of reduced tensions offered some relief to global markets monitoring the situation closely. Qatar, the Gulf's biggest liquefied natural gas producer, had suspended activity at its facilities and declared force majeure on gas exports, with sources indicating a return to normal production could take at least a month.

The market reaction underscored how closely investors are tracking both geopolitical developments and sector-specific trends. Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, noted that intelligence from US military channels suggests Iran's conventional military capacity is deteriorating after significant naval losses and sustained airstrikes. He pointed to positive economic signals including solid US economic data and a strong jobs report as additional support for stock markets.

The gains in stock indexes were not uniform throughout trading sessions. Technology stocks experienced volatility, with some segments swinging between gains and losses. The potential for an Iran deal carries significant implications for energy prices and global supply chains, while the performance of chip stocks reflects broader confidence in technology sector fundamentals despite concerns about funding requirements for artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion.

hero.headline: Drones From Russia-Ukraine War Stray Into Neighboring Countries
hero.teaser: Unmanned aircraft launched by both sides in the conflict are veering off course and entering airspace of countries not involved in the war.
hero.body:
Unmanned aircraft deployed by both Russia and Ukraine during their conflict are veering off course and entering the airspace of neighboring countries. The errant drones have prompted citizens in nations not involved in the war to seek shelter as the wayward aircraft pass overhead.

The incidents highlight the spillover risks of the extensive drone warfare being conducted by both sides. Neither Russia nor Ukraine maintains full control over all unmanned aircraft once launched, creating hazards for neutral countries in the region. The situation has raised concerns about the broader impact of the conflict on regional security and civilian safety in countries along Ukraine's borders.

Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russian military and economic infrastructure used to support the war effort. Kyiv's forces have targeted ships, planes, airfields, oil refineries, fuel depots, pipelines, natural gas networks, and factories that manufacture military electronics and explosives. These strikes have forced Russia to concentrate its air defense systems in certain areas, leaving other regions extremely vulnerable or completely undefended.

Russia's air defense challenges have become so severe that the government has instructed its major banks and financial institutions to defend themselves against drone attacks. The Russian parliament passed a law allowing banks including Sberbank, the country's largest, and other financial institutions to operate defense systems and arm staff against drones without requiring special forces involvement. These organizations would bear the costs of their own defenses.

Alexander Shokhin, head of Russia's most powerful business lobby, told Vladimir Putin that companies were willing to purchase heavier weapons and electronic defense systems to protect themselves against drone strikes.

The conflict has also strained diplomatic relations in the region. Russia announced a campaign of "systematic" strikes on Kyiv targeting the Ukrainian capital's "decision-making centres" and urged foreign citizens and diplomats to leave the city. Moscow also encouraged residents to avoid public buildings. However, Ukraine dismissed these threats as "blackmail," and its allies largely ignored the warning. Germany and Norway summoned Russian ambassadors to deliver formal reprimands. Nearly 50 countries at the United Nations condemned what they characterized as Russian threats to diplomatic institutions and embassies in Kyiv.

Meanwhile, international support for Ukraine continues. The Czech Republic announced that its initiative to supply large-caliber ammunition to Ukraine has secured contracts to deliver approximately one million rounds in 2026. The country delivered about 1.5 million rounds in 2024 and 1.8 million in the previous year. Financing of nearly one billion euros has been secured so far this year, supported by multiple donor countries including Denmark, the Netherlands, and Germany, as well as yields from frozen Russian assets provided by the European Commission. Additional funding may come from the European Union's 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine.

cards.headline: Man Shot at Kenya Protest Against US Ebola Quarantine Center
cards.teaser: A person was shot during demonstrations against a planned US-run Ebola treatment facility.
cards.body:
A man was shot in the head during a protest in Nanyuki, a town in central Kenya about 120 miles from Nairobi. The demonstration took place near Laikipia airbase, the proposed site of a US-run Ebola quarantine facility. Dozens of protesters gathered to oppose the center, with some wearing protective equipment and carrying a coffin marked "Ebola."

Police used teargas to disperse the demonstrators as tensions escalated. Protesters expressed concerns about the risk of cross-border infection from the treatment center and criticized the Kenyan government's lack of transparency regarding the facility's operations and safety protocols.

cards.headline: Man Arrested After Stabbing in Belfast
cards.teaser: Police in Northern Ireland arrested a suspect in his 30s following an attack that was recorded and circulated online.
cards.body:
Police in Belfast arrested a man in his 30s in connection with a stabbing attack in the city. The suspect is Sudanese, according to police. Video of the assault was recorded and spread rapidly on social media.

Northern Ireland police have appealed for calm following the incident. Officials described the attack as brutal and called on the public to avoid speculation. The stabbing has prompted calls for protests, and authorities are working to prevent tensions from escalating further in the community.

cards.headline: Iran Says Its World Cup Tickets Have Been Revoked
cards.teaser: Iran's soccer federation said its tickets for the tournament were canceled, blaming US interference.
cards.body:
Iran's football federation announced that its World Cup ticket allocation for the group stage has been revoked just days before the tournament begins. The federation did not specify who was responsible for revoking the tickets but blamed the United States, which is co-hosting the World Cup.

The move reflects broader tensions between Iran and the United States. The ticket revocation comes amid ongoing conflict involving Iran, creating diplomatic complications for the country's participation in the international sporting event.

hero.headline: US Army helicopter crew rescued after crash near Strait of Hormuz
hero.body:
Two crew members of a US Army Apache helicopter were rescued after their aircraft went down near the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman on Monday. An unmanned vessel recovered the crew from the water, according to US officials who confirmed the details to CBS News.

President Trump stated that the two pilots were "fine" following the incident. Trump also expressed optimism about ongoing negotiations with Iran during comments about the crash. The cause of the helicopter going down has not been disclosed by officials.

The Strait of Hormuz is a strategic waterway located between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. A significant portion of the world's oil supply passes through this passage, making it a critical global shipping route.

The rescue operation involved an uncrewed sea drone that was operating in the area. The use of unmanned maritime vessels in rescue operations represents an expanding capability for US military forces deployed in the region. The Apache is a twin-engine attack helicopter used by the US Army for various combat and support missions.

The incident occurred amid heightened tensions in the Middle East. In a related incident, a US fighter jet fired a missile that struck a sanctioned oil tanker off Oman. The crew of the oil tanker made a distress call after being hit by the missile and were subsequently rescued.

The Strait of Hormuz area has experienced increased US military activity in recent years as Washington maintains a substantial presence in the Persian Gulf region. The successful recovery of the helicopter crew using unmanned technology demonstrates the growing capabilities available to US forces operating in these waters.

Both crew members were reported to be in stable condition following their recovery from the water. The incident highlights the risks faced by military personnel operating in one of the world's most strategically important and contested maritime regions.

cards.headline: House votes on $70 billion immigration enforcement funding bill
cards.teaser: Congress moves toward approving funding for ICE and border agencies through the end of Trump's presidency.
cards.body:
The House prepared to vote on a Republican immigration bill that would provide $70 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies. The measure would fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection through the remainder of the Trump presidency.

The vote represents the end of a months-long impasse in Congress over immigration funding. The bill represents a significant increase in resources for federal immigration enforcement operations.

cards.headline: US missile strikes sanctioned oil tanker off Oman
cards.teaser: Crew of a sanctioned oil tanker were rescued after it was hit by a missile fired from a US fighter jet.
cards.body:
A US fighter jet fired a missile that struck a sanctioned oil tanker operating off the coast of Oman. The crew issued a distress call seeking assistance following the strike.

All crew members were successfully rescued from the vessel after the incident.

cards.headline: Israel continues air strikes on Lebanese city despite Iranian warning
cards.teaser: Iran warned Israel that it could resume hostilities if attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon do not stop.
cards.body:
Israeli air strikes have targeted the Lebanese city of Tyre as Iran issued a stark warning to Israel. On Monday, Iran cautioned that it could resume hostilities if attacks on Hezbollah, its Lebanese ally, do not cease.

The strikes on Tyre proceeded despite Iran's statement, escalating tensions in the region. Israel has been conducting military operations against Hezbollah positions in Lebanon, prompting the Iranian warning about potential retaliation.

cards.headline: Man jailed for stabbing partner 31 times and setting house on fire
cards.teaser: Clifton George killed Annabel Rook before starting a fire at their home in north London.
cards.body:
A man was sentenced to prison after murdering his partner and causing an explosion at their home. Clifton George stabbed Annabel Rook 31 times before setting fire to their house in north London.

The fire George started caused significant damage to the property. George was convicted of murder and arson following the attack on Rook.

cards.headline: Carer sentenced for killing her mother
cards.teaser: Stefania Glowka received a prison sentence after pleading guilty to manslaughter based on diminished responsibility.
cards.body:
A carer has been jailed for killing her mother. Stefania Glowka pleaded guilty to manslaughter based on diminished responsibility, a partial defense that applies when a defendant's mental functioning was substantially impaired at the time of the offense.

Glowka told authorities she could no longer continue in her caregiving role. The court accepted her plea, which reduced the charge from murder to manslaughter.

cards.headline: West Ham football regulator reviews allegations against club co-chair
cards.teaser: Multiple women accuse billionaire David Sullivan of abusing his power, in some cases when they were in their late teens.
cards.body:
The football regulator is reviewing serious allegations against West Ham co-chair David Sullivan following reports from multiple women who accused him of sexual misconduct and abusing his power. Some of the alleged incidents involved women in their late teens.

Sullivan, a 77-year-old billionaire who owns 38.8% of the club, stepped down as director and co-chair ahead of the allegations becoming public. The football regulator could potentially force him to sell his stake in West Ham United as part of its review.

cards.headline: Oil Prices Decline After Israel and Iran Agree to Halt Strikes
cards.teaser: Crude prices fell as the two nations agreed to stop attacking each other, easing concerns about broader regional conflict.
cards.body:
Oil prices retreated after Israel and Iran agreed to halt strikes against each other, reducing fears of a wider conflict that could disrupt supplies. The agreement brought relief to energy markets that had seen prices spike as the military confrontation intensified.

The decline in crude prices reflected decreased risk premiums that traders had built into oil futures during the height of tensions. Energy markets had been closely monitoring the potential for attacks on oil infrastructure and shipping lanes in the Persian Gulf region, which handles a significant portion of global petroleum exports.

cards.headline: OpenAI Tests Market Appetite Ahead of Planned Stock Offering
cards.teaser: The artificial intelligence company is gauging investor interest as it prepares for a public offering alongside SpaceX and Anthropic.
cards.body:
OpenAI has confidentially filed to go public on the US stock market, according to an announcement from the company. The artificial intelligence giant is expected to be valued at more than $850 billion, making it one of the most highly valued listings in market history. OpenAI noted it has not decided on timing for the IPO, acknowledging there are advantages to remaining private for now.

The planned offering comes as SpaceX and Anthropic also prepare to enter public markets, concentrating major technology IPOs in a compressed timeframe. Analysts are questioning whether investor appetite and market capacity can sustain multiple large offerings from AI companies simultaneously.

cards.headline: US Exports Rose in April as Iran War Boosted Oil Demand
cards.teaser: Commerce Department data showed export growth slightly outpaced import growth last month.
cards.body:
US exports increased in April, with the growth rate exceeding that of imports, according to Commerce Department data. The war with Iran contributed to higher demand for American oil exports as global energy markets sought alternative supplies.

The trade figures showed that American producers benefited from disruptions to Middle Eastern oil flows, with foreign buyers turning to US sources. The export gains reflected both higher volumes and elevated prices for petroleum products as the conflict created supply concerns in global markets.

cards.headline: JPMorgan Chase Plans to Deploy AI Agents This Year
cards.teaser: The nation's largest bank is preparing to roll out autonomous artificial intelligence systems.
cards.body:
JPMorgan Chase announced plans to deploy more powerful AI agents in 2026 as the financial institution accelerates its adoption of artificial intelligence technology. The bank is moving toward autonomous systems that can perform tasks with less human oversight.

CEO Jamie Dimon has indicated the bank will increase hiring of AI talent to support the technology rollout. The moves come as major financial institutions compete to implement AI systems that can improve efficiency and reduce operational costs across various banking functions.

cards.headline: Netherlands Blocks US Acquisition of National ID System Provider
cards.teaser: Dutch authorities stopped a $115 million deal involving a company that handles the country's identification infrastructure.
cards.body:
The Netherlands blocked a US technology company from acquiring a Dutch firm that manages the national identification system, citing threats to public interest. The $115 million transaction was halted by Dutch authorities concerned about foreign control of sensitive government infrastructure.

The decision reflects growing scrutiny of cross-border acquisitions involving companies that handle critical public services and data. European regulators have increasingly intervened in deals where foreign ownership could affect national security or essential government functions.

cards.headline: Iran Conflict Tests Dubai's Economic Model Built on Trade and Travel
cards.teaser: The Persian Gulf city's dependence on commerce and tourism has become a vulnerability as war affects regional stability.
cards.body:
Dubai's economy is facing fresh challenges as regional tensions create uncertainty for its core industries. The emirate's business model depends heavily on trade and tourism, sectors vulnerable to military instability in the Persian Gulf. Aviation, financial services, and retail have all felt the impact as businesses and travelers reassess the risks of operating in the region.

The conflict threatens advantages Dubai has long relied on—its reputation for stability and its role as a neutral commercial hub. Recent developments, including pauses in strikes between Iran and Israel, have provided some relief to oil markets and regional commerce, but the underlying tensions remain a significant concern for the emirate's economic outlook.

cards.headline: Nintendo unveils Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2
cards.teaser: Nintendo announced a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 console, scheduled to launch in 2026.
cards.body:
Nintendo announced a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time during its Nintendo Direct presentation on Tuesday. The game will launch in 2026 for Nintendo Switch 2. This marks the first major Zelda release since Echoes of Wisdom in 2024.

Further details about the remake will be shared at a later date.

cards.headline: US Navy completes first drone boat rescue of helicopter crew at sea
cards.teaser: The US Navy's Task Force 59 successfully rescued a downed helicopter crew using an autonomous drone boat near the Strait of Hormuz.
cards.body:
An uncrewed vessel successfully rescued two crew members from a US Apache helicopter that crashed at sea near the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. US officials confirmed the operation to CBS News, marking the first time a drone boat has been used for such a recovery mission.

The rescue demonstrates the practical application of autonomous maritime technology in emergency situations. Task Force 59, which has been integrating uncrewed vessels into naval operations, achieved this milestone through the successful deployment of its drone boat systems.

cards.headline: Square Enix announces Kingdom Hearts IV for multiple platforms
cards.teaser: Square Enix revealed Kingdom Hearts IV with a new gameplay trailer, confirming simultaneous launches on consoles and PC including Nintendo Switch 2.
cards.body:
Square Enix announced Kingdom Hearts IV during a Nintendo Direct presentation. The game will release on Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Xbox, and PC simultaneously. A new gameplay trailer provided the first look at the upcoming installment.

The announcement marks the return of a mainline Kingdom Hearts entry after a significant gap in the franchise. However, Square Enix has not yet revealed a specific release date for the game.

cards.headline: Apple introduces subscription bundles to App Store
cards.teaser: Apple expanded its App Bundles feature to allow developers to create discounted subscription packages with partner apps.
cards.body:
Apple is expanding its App Bundles feature to let developers team up on discounted subscription packages. Multiple developers can now partner together to offer their apps at reduced prices compared to buying individual subscriptions.

This addition to the App Store gives developers a new way to collaborate and cross-promote their services. Users benefit from bundled pricing similar to streaming service offerings, while developers can reach audiences through partnership arrangements.

cards.headline: Apple to remove low-engagement apps from App Store
cards.teaser: Apple announced plans to begin removing apps from the App Store that the company considers stale, low-value, or unable to attract users.
cards.body:
Apple stated it may start removing existing applications from the App Store if they fail to attract users or if the company considers them stale or low-value. This marks a shift in how Apple curates its app ecosystem, with user engagement now serving as a key factor in determining whether apps remain available on the platform.

The policy could affect thousands of apps currently listed in the store that receive minimal downloads or active use. Developers whose applications fall below engagement thresholds may face removal, fundamentally changing the landscape for lesser-known or niche applications.

cards.headline: High-severity Linux vulnerability traced to single character error
cards.teaser: A use-after-free bug in Linux that can bypass sandbox defenses was caused by a single errant character in the code.
cards.body:
Security researchers identified a high-severity vulnerability in the Linux operating system that originated from a single character error in the codebase. The bug is classified as a use-after-free vulnerability, a type of memory management flaw that occurs when a program continues to use memory after it has been freed.

The vulnerability can be exploited to evade sandbox defenses, which are security measures designed to isolate applications from the rest of the system. The discovery highlights how small coding errors can create significant security risks in widely used operating systems.

hero.headline: Browns guard Joel Bitonio retires after 12 NFL seasons
hero.teaser: The longtime Cleveland left guard announced his retirement on Tuesday.
hero.body:
Joel Bitonio announced his retirement from the NFL on Tuesday after spending 12 seasons with the Cleveland Browns. The left guard played his entire professional career with the franchise after being drafted by the team.

Bitonio was a fixture on the Browns offensive line throughout his career, serving as a cornerstone player for the organization. His departure leaves a significant hole on the Cleveland roster heading into the next season as the team continues to reshape its roster.

The timing of Bitonio's retirement comes during a period of significant change for the Browns organization. The team recently underwent major restructuring, including the firing of head coach Kevin Stefanski in January and the hiring of former Baltimore Ravens offensive coordinator Todd Monken as his replacement.

The Browns have also made notable moves on the personnel front. The organization completed a blockbuster trade involving star edge rusher Myles Garrett, sending him to the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for linebacker Jared Verse and multiple draft selections. Garrett, a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and seven-time Pro Bowl selection, had requested a trade following the team's disappointing 3-14 season in 2024.

Despite signing a significant contract extension worth $204.8 million with the Browns, Garrett expressed frustration with the franchise's direction and opted for a fresh start with a team positioned for championship contention. The Rams, who reached last season's NFC Championship Game, were willing to make the aggressive trade to acquire the elite defensive player.

General Manager Andrew Berry addressed the difficult decision, stating that the organization faced a crossroads regarding whether to retain their generational talent or make moves they believed were best for the long-term future of the franchise. The Browns ultimately decided to move forward with the trade, acquiring Verse along with draft picks in 2027, 2028, and 2029.

Verse, 25, was a first-round selection by the Rams in 2024 and earned Defensive Rookie of the Year honors. The standout pass rusher was also selected to the Pro Bowl this past season and has accumulated 12 career sacks along with 22 tackles for loss.

The Rams' acquisition of Garrett marks a significant offensive move for the organization, which has a history of making bold trades to pursue championship aspirations. The team previously acquired quarterback Matthew Stafford in 2021 and won the Super Bowl in his first season with the franchise.

With Bitonio's retirement and other roster changes underway, the Browns are entering a new era under head coach Todd Monken with a substantially different roster composition than previous seasons.

cards.headline: Caitlin Clark hits game-winning three-pointer for Fever with 1.2 seconds left
cards.teaser: The rookie guard's late shot gave Indiana a 78-76 victory over Washington on Monday night.
cards.body:
Caitlin Clark delivered a clutch three-pointer with 1.2 seconds remaining to lift the Indiana Fever past the Washington Mystics 78-76 on Monday night. The rookie guard's shot proved to be the decisive moment in a tightly contested matchup.

Following the game, Clark reflected on her performance, noting she was able to block out distractions during the crucial moment. The shot exemplified another memorable play from the former Iowa standout's first season in professional basketball.

cards.headline: Spurs beat Knicks in Game 3 to cut NBA Finals deficit to 2-1
cards.teaser: The San Antonio Spurs defeated the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Monday night to pull within 2-1 in the NBA Finals.
cards.body:
Victor Wembanyama recorded 32 points, eight rebounds and six assists Monday night as the San Antonio Spurs defeated the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden. The win marked Wembanyama's first NBA Finals victory and helped the Spurs return to what the team called its brand of basketball, cutting the Knicks' series lead to 2-1.

The Spurs dominated the second half at the free throw line, shooting 24 attempts compared to eight for the Knicks. Knicks coach Mike Brown criticized the officiating disparity after the game, saying he never expected to see such an imbalance during the Finals. San Antonio's defensive intensity kept them alive in the championship series after falling behind 2-0 in the first two games.

cards.headline: FIFA revokes Iran fan ticket allocation for World Cup games in United States
cards.teaser: The governing body pulled tickets for all three of Iran's group stage matches, according to the Iranian football federation.
cards.body:
FIFA has revoked the ticket allocation for Iranian fans attending the country's three World Cup group stage matches in the United States, according to Iran's national football federation. The announcement was made on Tuesday.

The decision eliminates all tickets that had been previously reserved for Iranian supporters at these games during the tournament.

cards.headline: Teen golfer Miles Russell qualifies for U.S. Open with Charlie Woods as caddie
cards.teaser: The teenage player made it through qualifying with Tiger Woods' son carrying his bag.
cards.body:
Miles Russell, 17 and the world's No. 10 amateur, earned one of four spots available at the U.S. Open qualifier in Florida on Monday. He survived a playoff to secure his place in the field, which will compete next week at Shinnecock Hills.

Charlie Woods, son of three-time U.S. Open champion Tiger Woods, served as Russell's caddie during the 36-hole qualifier. The two are close friends and commercial agency partners who will both attend Florida State to play college golf.

cards.headline: Texas court schedules Sorsby NCAA trial for February
cards.teaser: The case involving the Texas Tech quarterback will begin two weeks after the college football championship game.
cards.body:
A Texas court set the trial date for Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby's lawsuit against the NCAA to begin in February. The trial will start two weeks after the College Football Playoff national championship game is scheduled to be played.

The timing places the trial in the middle of the offseason for college football. Sorsby is currently the quarterback for Texas Tech and is pursuing legal action against the NCAA.

cards.headline: Emma Raducanu wins opening match at Queen's Club
cards.teaser: The British player defeated Anna Blinkova in straight sets in a rain-delayed match.
cards.body:
Emma Raducanu won her opening match of the grass-court season at Queen's Club, defeating Russia's Anna Blinkova 6-0 6-3 to advance to the second round. The commanding performance showcased the British number one's form on grass as she prepares for Wimbledon.

The victory gives Raducanu an encouraging start to her preparations for the major championship at the All England Club.

hero.headline: Scott Pelley Firing Intensifies Scrutiny of CBS News Leadership Under Bari Weiss
hero.body:
CBS News is grappling with significant internal turmoil following Scott Pelley's termination from 60 Minutes and his subsequent public criticism of the network's new leadership. The veteran journalist's firing has raised fresh questions about the management approach of Bari Weiss, who took over as editor-in-chief in October.

Pelley was dismissed after openly clashing with network leadership over recent staff cuts at 60 Minutes. During a heated Monday meeting with newly appointed executive editor Nick Bilton and other CBS executives, Pelley criticized Weiss directly. "She's murdering 60 Minutes," he said. "She does not love this place. She was brought in to kill it and is doing exactly that." Bilton subsequently sent Pelley a termination message that same evening, citing his conduct in the meeting as grounds for dismissal "for cause."

The cuts that triggered the confrontation were substantial. Last week, CBS News management fired the show's executive producer, executive editor, and two correspondents, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi, without providing specific reasons for the terminations. The firings shocked staff members who had anticipated changes but not this level of upheaval.

Weiss arrived at CBS News from Free Press, a media startup she founded after leaving print journalism. Her appointment marked a significant departure from the network's traditional hiring practices for senior news positions, which typically involve journalists with extensive broadcast television experience. Her lack of television background has become a focal point of criticism as the network navigates these personnel changes.

The situation at CBS News reflects the broader challenges facing traditional broadcast journalism. Networks are adapting to changing media consumption patterns and facing considerable business pressures. Paramount, CBS's parent company, has itself encountered difficulties, including pending merger arrangements that have drawn regulatory attention.

Pelley's willingness to speak publicly about his firing represents an unusual level of discord for a network that has historically handled personnel matters privately. The public nature of his departure, combined with his subsequent comments, suggests deeper organizational tensions that may complicate efforts to stabilize the division.

The timing is particularly consequential for 60 Minutes. The program is now operating with significantly reduced correspondent resources. With Anderson Cooper already announcing his departure earlier this year and Pelley now terminated, the show heads into its 59th season with only three full-time correspondents: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, and L Jon Wertheim. Norah O'Donnell contributes to the program as well.

Bilton acknowledged the scale of change in his message to staff, writing that he would provide "unyielding support" for the team and their journalism as the program moves forward. How CBS leadership addresses this controversy will likely shape the network's news operations and internal culture significantly in the coming months.

cards.headline: Paramount Accuses Netflix of Campaign to Block Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
cards.teaser: Paramount claims Netflix is conducting an aggressive effort to undermine its planned $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery through regulatory pressure.
cards.body:
Paramount's top lawyer accused Netflix of launching what the company described as a panic-level scorched-earth campaign to poison regulators and stakeholders against Paramount's pending merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. The allegation suggests Netflix views the combined entity as a significant competitive threat to its streaming dominance.

The merger, valued at $111 billion, would unite two major entertainment companies with substantial film studios and streaming platforms. Netflix previously acquired Warner Bros.'s streaming and studios businesses in a separate transaction, making the competitive dynamics between the companies particularly complex.

cards.headline: Jay-Z Announces Paris and Los Angeles Concerts for 30th Anniversary Tour
cards.teaser: The rapper will perform at Stade de France in Paris on September 10 and at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles on October 23 as part of his anniversary celebration.
cards.body:
Jay-Z revealed two additional concerts as part of his ongoing 30th anniversary celebration, with performances scheduled in Paris and Los Angeles later this year. The Paris show will take place at Stade de France on September 10, while the Los Angeles concert is set for SoFi Stadium on October 23.

The announcement extends the rapper's milestone tour celebrating three decades in the music industry. Both venues are among the largest in their respective cities, with SoFi Stadium in particular known for hosting major entertainment events since opening in 2020.

cards.headline: Anna Faris Says Scary Movie 6 Cut Melania Trump Parody Scene
cards.teaser: The actress revealed that her portrayal of character Cindy as a MAGA supporter mocking Melania Trump was removed from the film despite her efforts to include it.
cards.body:
Anna Faris revealed in an interview with Dexerto that filmmakers removed a scene from Scary Movie 6 featuring her character Cindy Campbell parodying Melania Trump. Faris had advocated for the character to embody a classic MAGA supporter throughout production of the sixth installment in the long-running spoof franchise.

Scary Movie 6 recently earned a $54 million opening weekend at the domestic box office, marking the film's debut atop the charts. The comedy continues the series' tradition of satirizing horror films and aspects of popular culture.

cards.headline: Accenture Acquires Influencer Agency Whalar to Expand Marketing Operations
cards.teaser: The consulting giant purchased the creator and influencer agency to strengthen its Accenture Song marketing division.
cards.body:
Accenture completed its acquisition of Whalar, a creator and influencer agency, as part of efforts to expand the scale of its marketing arm, Accenture Song. Whalar co-CEOs Emma Harman and Jo Cronk will join Accenture Song while continuing to lead Whalar in their current positions.

The transaction separates Whalar from its former parent company, Whalar Group, which will operate as an independent entity following the deal. Accenture, a major consulting and professional services company, has been building out its creative and marketing capabilities through strategic acquisitions in recent years.

cards.headline: BBC Appoints Rhodri Talfan Davies as Deputy Director General
cards.teaser: Davies will serve as second-in-command to Director General Matt Brittin after previously serving as interim chief of the broadcaster.
cards.body:
The BBC named Rhodri Talfan Davies as its deputy director general, placing him in the second-highest position at the British broadcaster. Davies previously served as interim chief of the BBC before Matt Brittin was selected for the top role.

Brittin officially joined the BBC as director general last month after working as president of EMEA business and operations at Google. The appointment of Davies provides continuity in BBC leadership while establishing the management structure under Brittin's tenure.

cards.headline: Cocomelon Producer Releases UCLA Research Guide Addressing Content Concerns
cards.teaser: Moonbug Entertainment partnered with UCLA's Center for Scholars and Storytellers to address criticism that its preschool programming is overstimulating or addictive.
cards.body:
Moonbug Entertainment, the studio behind the hit preschool series Cocomelon, has partnered with UCLA's Center for Scholars and Storytellers to develop a media guide grounded in academic research. The guide directly addresses growing concerns that Cocomelon's fast-paced format may overstimulate young viewers or foster addictive viewing habits.

The company has defended its content creation practices, emphasizing its careful approach throughout the production process. The UCLA-researched guide aims to provide parents with evidence-based information about how the popular series affects child development and viewing behaviors.

hero.headline: Speaker Johnson meets with Trump as intelligence surveillance deadline looms
hero.teaser: Speaker Mike Johnson met with President Trump amid Democratic opposition to acting intelligence chief Bill Pulte that threatens foreign surveillance law reauthorization.
hero.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson met with President Trump on Tuesday morning as Democrats expressed serious concerns about Trump's appointment of Bill Pulte as acting Director of National Intelligence, threatening efforts to renew surveillance powers scheduled to expire at the end of the week.

The appointment has created a significant obstacle to reauthorizing Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which allows U.S. intelligence agencies to collect communications of foreign targets operating outside the country without a warrant. Congress faces a June 12 deadline to renew the authority.

Pulte, currently head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and a major Republican donor, has no intelligence background. His selection came days after Tulsi Gabbard departed from the DNI role. Senior Democrats immediately warned the appointment could collapse the fragile bipartisan agreement needed to extend Section 702.

Mark Warner, the Democratic vice-chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, criticized Pulte's qualifications. "What qualifications from my standpoint does Mr Pulte bring to the office? Well, he has shown that he is willing to do anything that President Trump wants, legal or otherwise," Warner said during a hearing Tuesday. In a subsequent interview, Warner stated that Pulte's appointment had upended what he described as an already difficult renewal process, saying "I do not have the confidence I had yesterday."

Democrats have made clear that support for a Section 702 extension could collapse unless Trump reconsiders the appointment. Warner reportedly asked Senate Majority Leader John Thune to use his influence with the White House to reverse the decision.

Thune offered a notably cool response to Trump's pick. He told reporters that the nation does not need a "weaponized" intelligence director and warned that Pulte would face "a lengthy road ahead" if nominated permanently.

Other senior Republicans have also pushed back. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate majority leader, said on Wednesday: "Anyone performing this role of such immense public trust must have the extensive national security experience required by statute, and no nominee who falls short of this requirement will earn my vote."

Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator from Connecticut, expressed concern that intelligence collection powers would now be controlled by someone with "a history of seeking out private information for political gain." Critics point to Pulte's tenure at the FHFA, where he leveled unproven fraud allegations against figures including Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook.

The current renewal bill, circulated by Senate Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton and Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, would extend Section 702 through June 2029 and include new penalties for intelligence abuses. The measure requires Democratic support to reach the 60-vote threshold needed for passage.

cards.headline: Senate leader says White House considering permanent intelligence chief amid surveillance law standoff
cards.teaser: Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the White House is seriously considering a long-term nominee to replace Bill Pulte as Director of National Intelligence, .
cards.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the White House is seriously considering a permanent nominee to replace Bill Pulte as Director of National Intelligence. The move could help resolve a Democratic blockade over foreign surveillance powers set to expire Friday.

The standoff centers on Trump's decision to appoint Pulte as acting DNI, which Democrats have opposed. A formal nominee would require Senate confirmation, including hearings before the Senate Intelligence Committee. The reauthorization of Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act authorities, which allow government surveillance on foreign targets, faces an end-of-week deadline.

cards.headline: Vance says US and Israeli interests diverge on Iran policy
cards.teaser: Vice President Vance acknowledged differences between US and Israeli positions on the Middle East amid public disputes between Trump and Netanyahu.
cards.body:
Vice President Vance acknowledged divergent US and Israeli interests on the way forward in the Middle East during remarks on Monday. The comments came amid public disputes between President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rising concern about Israeli intelligence activities in America.

Vance said the US and Israel share many interests but have different perspectives on certain issues. The acknowledgment reflects growing tensions in the US-Israel relationship as the two countries navigate policy differences over the ongoing conflict with Iran and broader Middle East strategy.

cards.headline: Former Biden defense secretary says US Navy could reopen Strait of Hormuz
cards.teaser: Lloyd Austin said the US Navy has the capability to reopen the Strait of Hormuz but should do so only with international support.
cards.body:
Original Card Text (Unchanged)

Former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin said Monday that the United States Navy could reopen the Strait of Hormuz but should only undertake the effort with support from international allies. Austin, who served under former President Biden, made the remarks during an appearance at the HSBC Gulf Cooperation event.

The comments come as the ongoing Iran war continues to affect global energy markets and shipping routes. The Strait of Hormuz serves as a critical chokepoint for oil shipments, and any closure or disruption has significant implications for global energy supplies and prices.

---

Note: The additional source material provided does not contain substantive details about Austin's remarks or the substance of his comments beyond confirming he said the U.S. could reopen the strait with allied support. The sources reference other incidents (sea drone rescue, closure precedent) but don't expand on the core newsworthy statement in the original card. Therefore, the card text is returned unchanged.

cards.headline: House tax chair says he will not support reconciliation bill without tax provisions
cards.teaser: Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith warned he will not back the next reconciliation bill if it lacks tax measures.
cards.body:
Representative Jason Smith, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, warned he will not support the next reconciliation bill unless it includes tax provisions. Smith also said he is still waiting to hear from the speaker on the matter.

The statement signals potential friction within Republican ranks over the content of upcoming budget reconciliation legislation. Reconciliation bills allow certain fiscal measures to pass the Senate with a simple majority, making them a key tool for advancing tax and spending priorities.

cards.headline: Nearly 60 percent expect gas prices to rise over next year, poll finds
cards.teaser: A new Reuters/Ipsos poll found 59 percent of Americans expect gas prices to increase as the Iran war continues to affect energy markets.
cards.body:
Nearly six in ten American adults expect gas prices to increase over the next year, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday. The survey of 4,531 respondents found that 59 percent anticipate higher prices at the pump.

The poll reflects broader public concerns about energy costs. The ongoing conflict with Iran has created uncertainty in global oil markets, with potential disruptions to supply routes and production contributing to price volatility across the country.

cards.headline: Former Interior secretary Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: Deb Haaland, who served as Interior secretary under President Biden, won the Democratic nomination for New Mexico governor.
cards.body:
I need to flag a significant error in the original card text: it states that Deb Haaland "will face the Republican nominee in November's general election for the seat currently held by Governor Gavin Newsom."

This is incorrect. Gavin Newsom is the Governor of California, not New Mexico. Haaland is running for governor of New Mexico, where the current governor is someone else entirely.

The source material provided doesn't contain detailed information about the New Mexico gubernatorial race beyond confirming Haaland won the Democratic primary and could make history as the first female Native American governor.

Here is the corrected card:

Deb Haaland won the New Mexico Democratic primary for governor on Tuesday. Haaland served as Interior secretary in the Biden administration before entering the gubernatorial race. If elected in November's general election, she would make history as the first female Native American governor in the United States.
